title: factor derivative and determine intervals
stem: A differentiable function f has f'(x)=(x+2)(x-1) on (-4,4). On which intervals is f increasing, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: f increases only on (-2,1), where the two factors have opposite signs.
choices.rationale: Opposite factor signs make f' negative between the roots, so f decreases there.

choices.label: B
choices.text: f increases on (-4,-2) and (1,4), where both derivative factors have the same sign.
choices.rationale: Correct: The product is positive for x<-2 and x>1, negative between the roots, and zero only at the roots. f increases where f'>0.

choices.label: C
choices.text: f increases on all of (-4,4) because f' has two zeros.
choices.rationale: Zeros split the domain into sign intervals; they do not make f positive everywhere.

choices.label: D
choices.text: f increases only at x=-2 and x=1 because f'=0 there.
choices.rationale: At the two isolated zeros the instantaneous slope is zero; intervals of increase come from positive derivative signs.

title: factor derivative and determine intervals (variant 1)
stem: Suppose g'(x)=-(x+3)(x-2) for every x in (-5,4). Which description of g is supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: g decreases on (-3,2) because the two factors have opposite signs there.
choices.rationale: The leading minus sign reverses the sign of the negative product between roots.

choices.label: B
choices.text: g increases on both outer intervals because a quadratic derivative is positive for large |x|.
choices.rationale: The leading minus sign makes the derivative negative outside the roots in this case.

choices.label: C
choices.text: g is constant on (-3,2) because g' vanishes at the interval's ends.
choices.rationale: The derivative vanishes only at two points, not throughout the open interval between them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: g increases on (-3,2) and decreases on (-5,-3) and (2,4).
choices.rationale: Correct: Inside (-3,2) the product (x+3)(x-2) is negative, so its negative is positive. On either outer interval the product is positive and g' negative.

title: factor derivative and determine intervals (variant 2)
stem: A differentiable h has h'(x)=x(x-2)(x+1) on (-3,3). Which intervals of increase follow from a sign analysis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: h increases on (-1,0) and (2,3), where the three-factor product is positive.
choices.rationale: Correct: Across roots -1,0,2, the cubic derivative signs are negative, positive, negative, positive. Positive signs give (-1,0) and (2,3).

choices.label: B
choices.text: h increases on (-3,-1) and (0,2), where the product is negative.
choices.rationale: A negative derivative means h decreases on those two intervals, not increases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: h increases on all intervals because h' has three real zeros.
choices.rationale: Roots identify sign boundaries; the derivative is negative on two of the four intervals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: h increases only at x=-1, 0, and 2.
choices.rationale: A derivative equal to zero at isolated points does not define an increasing interval.

title: factor derivative and determine intervals (variant 3)
stem: A differentiable p satisfies p'(x)=(x-1)²(x+2) on (-4,4). Where does p decrease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: p decreases on (-4,-2) and (1,4), since every derivative zero flips its sign.
choices.rationale: An even-multiplicity zero at 1 does not switch derivative sign.

choices.label: B
choices.text: p decreases on (-2,1), because x+2 is positive there.
choices.rationale: Both x+2 and the squared factor are positive on (-2,1), so p increases there.

choices.label: C
choices.text: p decreases on (-4,-2); the squared factor does not reverse the derivative's sign at x=1.
choices.rationale: Correct: (x-1)² is nonnegative and positive away from 1, so the sign comes from x+2. It is negative only for x<-2; the zero at 1 does not change sign.

choices.label: D
choices.text: p never decreases, because a squared factor makes p' nonnegative everywhere.
choices.rationale: The other factor x+2 is negative to the left of -2, making p' negative there.

title: read derivative sign representation
stem: A graph of f' lies above the x-axis on (-3,-1), below it on (-1,2), and above it on (2,4), crossing at -1 and 2. A student says f is negative on (-1,2). What is the justified conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: f is negative on (-1,2) because its derivative graph is below the axis.
choices.rationale: A negative derivative means negative slope, not necessarily negative function values.

choices.label: B
choices.text: f decreases on (-1,2); the sign of f' gives direction, but it does not determine whether f itself is positive or negative there.
choices.rationale: Correct: f'<0 throughout (-1,2), so f decreases. Derivative sign alone cannot determine the vertical position or sign of f.

choices.label: C
choices.text: f increases on (-1,2) because the graph of f' may be rising there.
choices.rationale: Whether f' itself rises does not change its negative sign on the stated interval.

choices.label: D
choices.text: f is constant on (-1,2) because f' equals zero at both ends.
choices.rationale: Zero derivative at isolated boundaries does not make f constant across the interval.

title: read derivative sign representation (variant 1)
stem: The derivative of a differentiable g is negative on (0,2) and positive on (2,5), with g(2)=7. Which comparison is certain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: g(1)>7 and g(4)>7; g decreases toward x=2 then increases away from it, but g(1) versus g(4) is undetermined.
choices.rationale: Correct: As x increases from 1 to 2, g falls to 7, so g(1)>7. As x increases from 2 to 4, g rises from 7, so g(4)>7. Their relative heights need rate magnitudes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: g(1)<7 and g(4)<7 because g' changes sign at 2.
choices.rationale: Both side values exceed the local minimum g(2)=7, not fall below it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: g(1)>g(4) because the negative derivative on (0,2) controls the whole interval.
choices.rationale: Derivative signs establish each comparison to g(2), but not between g(1) and g(4).

choices.label: D
choices.text: g(1)=g(4) because the intervals lie on opposite sides of x=2.
choices.rationale: Opposite sides of a minimum need not have equal function values without symmetry or rate information.

title: read derivative sign representation (variant 2)
stem: A differentiable function h has h'(x)>0 on (-4,0) and h'(x)<0 on (0,3). Which statement about h(-2), h(0), and h(2) must hold?

choices.label: A
choices.text: h(-2)<h(2)<h(0) must hold because -2<2.
choices.rationale: X-order alone cannot compare values across two intervals with opposite derivative signs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: h(-2)<h(0) and h(2)<h(0); the chart does not order h(-2) against h(2).
choices.rationale: Correct: A positive derivative up to 0 raises h from -2 to 0, and a negative derivative afterward lowers it from 0 to 2. The two side values can differ either way.

choices.label: C
choices.text: h(-2)>h(0)>h(2) because a positive derivative makes earlier values larger.
choices.rationale: A positive derivative makes later values greater on (-4,0), not earlier ones.

choices.label: D
choices.text: h(-2)=h(2) because the derivative signs switch at 0.
choices.rationale: A sign change at 0 establishes a peak, not symmetry of the two side values.

title: read derivative sign representation (variant 3)
stem: A graph shows q' positive for 1<x<3, zero at x=3, and negative for 3<x<6. A student concludes q is increasing on (1,6) because q'(3)=0. What correction is valid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: q increases on (1,3) and decreases on (3,6); one zero does not override the derivative signs on either side.
choices.rationale: Correct: The sign of q' is positive before 3 and negative afterward. Those signs determine the two monotonic intervals independently of the isolated zero.

choices.label: B
choices.text: q increases on all of (1,6) because a derivative can be zero at one point.
choices.rationale: A zero derivative at one point does not erase a negative derivative on the entire right interval.

choices.label: C
choices.text: q decreases on (1,3) because q' is above the axis there.
choices.rationale: A derivative graph above zero means q has positive slope and increases to the left of 3.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nothing can be inferred about monotonicity unless q values are also given.
choices.rationale: Derivative signs are sufficient to establish monotonic intervals when differentiability is given.

title: handle derivative sign across domain gaps
stem: A function f is differentiable wherever x≠2 and satisfies f'(x)=(x+1)/(x-2). Its domain includes both sides of x=2 but excludes x=2. Which monotonic intervals follow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: f increases on (-1,2) because the numerator is positive there.
choices.rationale: The denominator is negative on (-1,2), making the positive numerator produce a negative derivative.

choices.label: B
choices.text: f increases on (-infinity,-1) and (-1,infinity) because only the zero at -1 matters.
choices.rationale: The denominator changes sign at the excluded point 2, so the sign chart must split there.

choices.label: C
choices.text: f increases on (-infinity,-1) and (2,infinity), and decreases on (-1,2); the domain gap separates the last two intervals.
choices.rationale: Correct: The ratio signs across -1 and 2 are positive, negative, positive. x=2 is outside the domain, so monotonic intervals cannot be joined through it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: f decreases on both sides of x=2 because the denominator is zero there.
choices.rationale: A derivative undefined at one point does not force the same sign on both neighboring intervals.

title: handle derivative sign across domain gaps (variant 1)
stem: A differentiable g has g'(x)=(x-3)/(x+1) wherever x≠-1; g is undefined at -1. On which intervals is g decreasing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: g decreases on (-infinity,-1) and (3,infinity), because both factors share a sign there.
choices.rationale: Equal signs make a quotient positive, so g increases on the two outer intervals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: g decreases on (-infinity,3) as a single interval, crossing the excluded x=-1.
choices.rationale: A monotonic interval cannot contain the point -1 where g is not defined.

choices.label: C
choices.text: g never decreases because the derivative is a quotient rather than a product.
choices.rationale: A quotient can be negative; its sign is determined by numerator and denominator signs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: g decreases on (-1,3) only, where the numerator and denominator have opposite signs.
choices.rationale: Correct: For x<-1 the ratio is positive, for -1<x<3 it is negative, and for x>3 it is positive. The domain gap at -1 prevents merging across it.

title: handle derivative sign across domain gaps (variant 2)
stem: A function h has h'(x)=(x+2)/(x-1) wherever x≠1, and h is undefined at 1. Which statement is warranted by the derivative?

choices.label: A
choices.text: h decreases on both intervals to the left of 1 because the denominator is negative there.
choices.rationale: For x<-2 both numerator and denominator are negative, making h' positive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: x=1 is a critical point because h' does not exist there, even though h itself is undefined.
choices.rationale: An excluded input is not a point of h, so it cannot be a critical point on its graph.

choices.label: C
choices.text: h increases throughout (-infinity,infinity) because h' is positive for large x.
choices.rationale: Positive derivative for some large x-values does not establish increase on intervals where h'<0.

choices.label: D
choices.text: h decreases on (-2,1) and increases on (-infinity,-2) and (1,infinity); x=1 is a domain break, not a critical point of h.
choices.rationale: Correct: Across -2 and 1, ratio signs are positive, negative, positive. A critical point must be in the function's domain; x=1 is excluded.

title: handle derivative sign across domain gaps (variant 3)
stem: A differentiable p has p'(x)=(x-2)/(x+4) except at x=-4, where p is also undefined. A student says p increases on (-infinity,2) because the numerator is negative there. Which correction is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: p increases on (-4,2) because a negative numerator always makes a quotient positive.
choices.rationale: On (-4,2), the denominator is positive while the numerator is negative, so p'<0.

choices.label: B
choices.text: p increases on all x<2 as one interval because x=-4 is just an isolated point.
choices.rationale: No monotonic interval can cross an input at which the function is undefined.

choices.label: C
choices.text: p increases on (-infinity,-4) and (2,infinity), but decreases on (-4,2); the quotient changes sign at the excluded x=-4.
choices.rationale: Correct: The ratio is positive for x<-4, negative for -4<x<2, and positive for x>2. The excluded point splits the domain and the derivative sign.

choices.label: D
choices.text: p decreases on both outer intervals because the numerator has a zero at x=2.
choices.rationale: A derivative zero at x=2 does not make the derivative negative on either outer interval.
